common_name: Miss Lemon Abelia (Compact Chartreuse-Yellow Variegated Abelia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Miss Lemon holds a compact, rounded habit and bright lemon-yellow foliage color, brightest with more direct sun.

directions: Miss Lemon is a compact abelia selected for vivid chartreuse-to-lemon-yellow foliage that holds its bright color through the growing season, providing continuous visual interest even between flushes of the small, fragrant, pale pink tubular flowers that open from late spring into fall and draw butterflies and hummingbirds. Its smaller, more rounded habit than older variegated abelia cultivars fits foundation plantings, mixed borders, and large containers without the size management larger abelias require. Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade — more direct sun brings out the brightest foliage color, while too much shade shifts the leaves toward a duller green-gold. It tolerates heat, humidity, and brief dry spells well once established, needing only an occasional thinning cut after flowering to keep the shape tidy.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Radiance bears clean white flowers against glossy dark green foliage on a compact, dense habit.

directions: Radiance produces an abundance of pure white, fragrant, trumpet-shaped flowers against glossy, dark green foliage, a cleaner and more solid-colored look than the many variegated abelia cultivars on the market, on a dense, compact, rounded shrub that needs little pruning to hold its shape. It flowers over a long season from late spring into fall and draws steady butterfly and hummingbird traffic throughout. Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; heavier bloom develops with more direct sun. Like other abelias it is tough and adaptable, tolerating heat, humidity, clay soil, and short dry spells once established, and needs only an occasional thinning cut after flowering to control size.

common_name: Anthony Waterer Spirea (Classic Crimson-Pink Flowered Spirea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; one of the oldest and most widely planted spirea cultivars, dating to the late 1800s and still a garden standard.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and shear off spent flower clusters to encourage a second flush of bloom later in the season. Anthony Waterer is a long-cultivated, classic spirea dating to the 1800s, bearing flat-topped clusters of deep crimson-pink flowers over blue-green foliage that often shows an attractive irregular cream variegation on some leaves, and new growth frequently emerges reddish before maturing to green. Its reliable bloom, tough constitution, and long garden history have kept it a staple of foundation plantings, mixed borders, and mass plantings for well over a century. Extremely tough and adaptable, tolerating drought, poor soil, heat, and urban conditions with minimal care; prune in late winter to shape and remove old wood, and shear after the first bloom flush for a fuller rebloom.

common_name: Magic Carpet Spirea (Compact Red-New-Growth Foliage Spirea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Magic Carpet stays lower and more compact than Goldflame, with new growth emerging bright red-orange before settling to gold-green.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, where the best foliage color develops. Magic Carpet is a compact foliage spirea with new growth that emerges a vivid orange-red before maturing to gold and then gold-green through summer, all set off by small clusters of soft pink flowers in early summer. Its low, dense, mounding habit stays under 2 feet, fitting foundation edges, rock gardens, and mass plantings where taller foliage spireas like Goldflame would be oversized. Shear lightly after the main bloom flush to refresh foliage color and encourage tidy new growth. Extremely tough and drought-tolerant once established, needing minimal care beyond an occasional light shaping.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Limemound holds a bright lime-gold foliage color through summer, with new growth tinged orange-red in spring.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun for the brightest foliage color. Limemound bears fine-textured, bright lime-gold leaves that emerge tinged with orange-red in spring, providing a long season of foliage interest well beyond its small clusters of pale pink flowers in early summer. Its low, dense, mounding habit fits foundation plantings, mixed borders, and mass groupings where a season-long chartreuse foliage accent is wanted alongside darker-leaved companions. Shear lightly after the main bloom flush to refresh color and maintain a tidy mounded shape. It is tough and drought-tolerant once established, asking for very little beyond occasional light shaping.
